common_name: Kew Blue Bluebeard (Deep Violet-Blue Compact Caryopteris)

planting.note: Plant in spring after the last hard frost so roots establish before summer heat arrives.

directions: An older, well-tested selection prized for its deep violet-blue flower clusters set against gray-green foliage from midsummer into fall. Cut the whole plant back hard to 6-8 inches each spring since flowers form on new wood, and skip fertilizer to keep growth compact and floriferous. Excellent for pollinator borders and mixed with ornamental grasses where its late-season color extends the bloom season. Tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, but resents wet winter feet.

common_name: Common Bluebeard (Caryopteris incana, Species Blue Mist Shrub)

planting.note: Set out after frost danger passes in a spot with sharp drainage and full sun.

directions: The East Asian parent species behind most garden Caryopteris hybrids, blooming later and slightly taller than the clandonensis cultivars with dense clusters of fringed lavender-blue flowers into early fall. It is more heat-tolerant but less cold-hardy than its hybrids, often dying back to the ground in colder zones and regrowing reliably from the crown. Grow in lean, well-drained soil and avoid overwatering, which promotes floppy growth and root rot. Valuable as a late nectar source for bees and butterflies when little else is blooming.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Petit Bleu Bluebeard (Dwarf Compact Blue Caryopteris)

planting.note: Ideal for small gardens and containers; plant in spring in fast-draining soil.

directions: A dwarf, dense-mounding selection bred to stay under two feet without flopping, making it useful for front-of-border plantings, low hedges, and large containers where full-size bluebeards outgrow the space. Sky-blue flower clusters cover the compact silvery-green mound from late summer into fall. Prune back hard each spring to maintain its tight habit and encourage the heaviest bloom, since flowers appear only on current-season wood. Performs best in lean, well-drained soil with minimal supplemental feeding.
sources: American Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants

common_name: Rocketman Russian Sage (Narrow Non-Flopping Upright Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil; avoid rich beds that cause legginess.

directions: A modern selection bred for a slim, rigid, columnar habit that resists the splaying and flopping common in older Russian sage cultivars, making it easier to place in tight border spaces without staking. Airy spikes of violet-blue flowers rise above finely cut silver-gray foliage from midsummer through fall and are highly attractive to bees. Cut stems back to a low woody framework in early spring once new growth begins, since bloom occurs on new wood. Extremely drought-tolerant once established and best left unfed in average to lean soils.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Lacey Blue Russian Sage (Compact Non-Flopping Dwarf Hybrid)

planting.note: Set plants in full sun and lean soil in spring; good candidate for front-of-border or containers.

directions: A patented dwarf selection valued for its dense, self-supporting habit and heavy display of deep violet-blue flower spikes on silvery, finely dissected foliage, staying tidy without staking or shearing. Best sited in lean, sharply drained soil since excess fertility or moisture leads to soft, weak stems. Cut the plant back nearly to the base in early spring to renew growth and maximize bloom, as flowers form on the current season's stems. A strong pollinator draw for bees and butterflies through the heat of summer.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Caucasian Sage (Perovskia abrotanoides, Species Russian Sage Relative)

planting.note: Plant in spring into gritty, fast-draining soil in a hot, sunny site.

directions: A shorter, more branching species native to rocky slopes of Central Asia and the Caucasus, notable as a parent of several modern compact Russian sage hybrids. Foliage is aromatic and deeply cut, and the plant produces the same haze of small violet-blue flowers on wiry stems from summer into fall, though it stays lower and denser than Perovskia atriplicifolia. Thrives in poor, gritty soil and needs no supplemental feeding; excess moisture or rich soil causes weak, sprawling growth. Cut back close to the woody base in early spring before new shoots emerge.
sources: Flora of Iran / Central Asia botanical references

common_name: Golden Germander (Woolly Yellow-Flowered Rock Garden Germander)

planting.note: Plant or direct sow in spring into gritty, low-fertility soil in full sun.

directions: A low, mat-forming Mediterranean sub-shrub covered in fine white wool that gives the foliage a silvery-gray cast, topped in summer by dense rounded heads of tiny yellow flowers that draw bees and other small pollinators. Ideal for rock gardens, gravel beds, and dry stone walls where its compact form and drought tolerance shine. Requires sharp drainage above all else; wet soil, especially in winter, quickly causes crown rot. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound tight and encourage repeat bloom.

planting.note: Set out after frost in a sunny spot with excellent drainage, such as a slope or raised bed.

directions: A low, spreading germander native to the Balearic Islands, forming a dense silvery-gray carpet of narrow, felted leaves studded with small lavender-pink flowers through summer. Its trailing habit makes it a favorite for cascading over rock walls, edging paths, and filling gaps between paving stones in hot, dry sites. Give it gritty, lean, sharply drained soil and avoid winter wet, which it tolerates poorly. Shear lightly after bloom to keep growth dense and to remove spent flower stems.
